d.title: Three ranking functions on the values 10, 10, 9
d.caption: **`row_number()` gives 1, 2, 3 — `rank()` gives 1, 1, 3 — `dense_rank()` gives 1, 1, 2.** Which is the whole distinction and the reason the wrong one is a quiet bug: **`row_number()` breaks ties arbitrarily, so “top 3 by score” silently drops one of two equal scores and the result is non-deterministic between runs.** Use `row_number()` when you need exactly one row per group, **`rank()` when the gap after a tie is meaningful, and `dense_rank()` when it is not.**

d.title: Each CTE is a named step you can read, test and reason about
d.caption: **The equivalent nested-subquery version is the same work and unreadable** — so this is a legibility argument rather than a performance one, and worth being precise about: **on PostgreSQL a plain CTE is no longer an optimisation fence, so the planner inlines it and the two forms usually produce the same plan.** Which removes the old reason to avoid them. The remaining practical advantage: **you can run a single CTE on its own to see what it returns**, where a nested subquery has to be extracted by hand first.

d.title: Five key choices, and UUID v7 is usually the right default
d.caption: **An auto-increment `BIGINT` is compact and index-friendly, and it leaks your volume — order 4,281 tells a competitor how many orders you have had.** A v4 UUID leaks nothing and **fragments the index, because random inserts land everywhere in the B-tree.** **v7 is time-ordered, so it keeps the UUID benefits with sequential locality** — which is why it is the default to reach for. And the warning on natural keys is the one that costs most to fix: **natural keys change, and then so does every reference to them.**

d.title: `CASCADE` on the wrong relationship is a data-loss incident
d.caption: **Deleting a customer should not silently delete their orders** — an order is a financial record with a life of its own, and `ON DELETE CASCADE` there turns one careless `DELETE` into an audit problem. The useful rule: **cascade down an ownership relationship where the child cannot exist without the parent — an order line without an order — and `RESTRICT` everywhere else, so the delete fails and somebody has to decide.** And `SET NULL` is the third option worth knowing: **it keeps the child and forgets the link**, which is right for an optional reference.

d.title: The leading-column rule is the one that catches people
d.caption: **An index on `(account_id, created_at)` does nothing for a query filtering on `created_at` alone** — a composite index is usable left to right, so the leading column must appear in the predicate. Which is why **two single-column indexes are not equivalent to one composite index, and one composite index is not equivalent to two.** The second row is the companion rule: **the index can satisfy `account_id` alone, so a separate index on it is redundant** — and an unused index still costs a write on every insert.

d.title: Four row factories, and `class_row` fails early when a column is renamed
d.caption: **`class_row` is the one to reach for in application code: it gives type checking, autocompletion, and an early failure when the query and the class disagree** — a renamed column raises at the row factory rather than producing a `None` that travels. The default tuple is the one to avoid in anything but a script: **`row[3]` rots the moment a column is inserted**, and nothing tells you. And `dict_row` is the middle ground — **named access with no schema**, so a typo'd key is still a `KeyError` at use.

d.title: A bare `except Exception` turns four different situations into one 500
d.caption: **A unique violation is a 409 the user can act on; a foreign-key violation is a 400; a serialisation failure is a retry; and a connection error is a 503 with a backoff.** Collapsing all four into a 500 throws away the only information that distinguishes them — **and the client cannot tell “you sent a duplicate” from “our database is down”.** The practical form is to catch the driver's specific exception types, **or inspect `e.sqlstate`, which is a documented five-character code and stable across versions.**

d.title: A transaction spans exactly the writes that must agree, and nothing slow
d.caption: **External calls belong outside it — or the transaction is open for the duration of someone else's outage, holding locks and a pooled connection while a payment gateway times out.** Which is the rule and its reason in one sentence. The practical shape: **validate and call out first, then open the transaction, write, and commit**; if the external call must happen after the write, **commit and then do it, accepting that the two can disagree** — and reconcile, rather than holding a transaction open to pretend they cannot.

d.title: A retried transaction re-runs everything inside it
d.caption: **So anything with an external effect must be outside the transaction — or idempotent, which is 14.3's territory and the harder of the two options.** The retry itself is narrow: **retry on a serialisation failure or a deadlock, which the database tells you about by code, and never on a constraint violation**, because that will fail identically every time. And the bound matters: **a few attempts with jitter, because a retry storm under contention makes the contention worse** — every retrying transaction is still competing for the same rows.

d.title: The loading strategy is a per-query decision, and the default is the N+1
d.caption: **`lazy="select"` is the default and it is the N+1 generator: each attribute access issues another query, at a point in the code far from the one that loaded the parent.** `selectinload` issues one extra query with an `IN` clause — **the right default for a collection** — and `joinedload` uses one query with a join, **which is right for a many-to-one and wrong for a collection, because the parent's columns are duplicated per child row.** And `raise` is the one worth knowing about: **it turns an accidental lazy load into an exception**, so the N+1 fails loudly in tests.

d.title: `select(Order.id, Order.total)` is Core semantics through the ORM's session
d.caption: **No instances are constructed, no identity-map entries are made, and nothing is tracked for changes** — which is most of what the ORM costs, removed by naming columns instead of a class. Worth knowing because it is the cheapest escape hatch: **the session, the connection and the transaction are all still yours**, so a reporting query inside an ORM application does not need a second access layer. The other two costs the ORM imposes: **a unit-of-work flush whose ordering you do not control, and an identity map that keeps every loaded row alive for the session's life.**

d.title: The third pattern works even when the ORM cannot help
d.caption: **Collect the keys, fetch them in one query, index them by key, then attach** — four steps, no eager-loading configuration, and it works across an HTTP boundary or a second data store where `selectinload` cannot reach. Which is why it is the general one: **the first two fixes are the ORM telling the database to do the work, and this one is you doing it.** The measured shape is the same in all three: **1 + N queries become 2**, and the second is a single `IN` over a de-duplicated key list.

d.title: Six queries where adding an index is the wrong instinct
d.caption: **`count(*)` must visit every row to check visibility, so no index makes it cheap — use an estimate from `pg_class` or keep a counter table.** The last row is the one that surprises: **a `WHERE status = 'active'` matching 60% of the table will not use an index, because random heap reads for most of the table are slower than a sequential scan** — and the fix is a **partial index on the rare value** rather than a better index on the common one. And the general shape: **three of the six are fixed by returning less, not by seeking faster.**

d.title: Autogenerate is a draft, not a migration
d.caption: **It misses server defaults, enum changes, index method choices and anything about data** — so the generated file is a starting point you are expected to edit, and treating it as output is how a migration drops a column it should have renamed. The two habits that follow: **read every generated migration before committing it**, and **write the data migration by hand**, because autogenerate compares schemas and has no idea a column's values need moving. And the one that saves an outage: **test the downgrade**, since the first time you need it will be the worst time to discover it was never run.

d.title: Two scenarios with the same cause: something scoped wrongly
d.caption: **A module-level `session = Session()` produces random `InvalidRequestError`s, objects from one user's request appearing in another's response, and sporadic deadlocks** — because a `Session` is a unit of work for one request and sharing it shares its identity map. The pool exhaustion is the mirror image: **requests hang for ~30 s and then fail with `QueuePool limit of size 5 overflow 10 reached`, because connections were checked out and never returned.** The rule in one line: **the engine is global and the session is per request.**

d.title: The async ORM removes the safety net that hid the decision
d.caption: **“Lazy loading just works” is what the sync ORM gave you, and the async one does not — so the loading strategy becomes a per-query decision you have to make.** Which sounds like a regression and is closer to an improvement: **in sync code the same laziness was issuing the same N+1, silently, and the async version raises instead.** The general lesson behind the grouped scenarios: **bound everything — the pool, the statement timeout, the result set and the retry count** — because every one of them is unbounded by default.
